summary: Describes how to carry location information about a user's access network, in civic or geospatial formats, inside RADIUS and Diameter messages. Because location data is sensitive, the document also discusses privacy concerns around distributing it.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a user connects through a mobile or public network, the equipment that connects them, the network access server, knows roughly where they are. The home network that bills and authorises the user usually does not.

This RFC defines attributes that let the access network pass location information back to the home network inside the RADIUS or Diameter messages that already happen during sign-in and accounting. It also defines attributes carrying the rules that say who may use the location afterwards and for how long, because knowing where someone is reveals a great deal about them.

questions: how does radius request location from a nas
subtitle: How an access network tells the home network where a user is, in RADIUS and Diameter messages.

tldr.problem: A home network that bills or authorises by location needs to know where the user is, but the access network has that information and the home network does not. Location data is also sensitive, so it cannot simply be passed around.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines seven RADIUS attributes: the operator that owns the access network, the location itself split into metadata and data, two attributes carrying the rules that govern further use of the data, and two attributes for saying what each side can do.
tldr.outcome: Location can ride along in the ordinary authentication and accounting exchanges, with the rules for who may keep it and for how long travelling with it. RFC 8559 later updated this document.

facts.label: Location-Information length
facts.value: At least 23 octets and at most 253 octets

today: RFC 5580 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 8559, which adds dynamic authorization proxying to the RADIUS protocol.

sections.title: Why Carry Location in RADIUS and Diameter
sections.content:
The document defines attributes within RADIUS and Diameter that can be used to convey location-related information within authentication and accounting exchanges.

Location information may be useful in a number of scenarios. Wireless networks, including wireless LAN, are being deployed in public places such as airports, hotels, shopping malls and coffee shops by a diverse set of operators such as cellular network operators, Wireless Internet Service Providers and fixed broadband operators. In these situations the home network may need to know the location of the user in order to enable location-aware billing, location-aware authorization or other location-aware services. Location information can also prove useful in other situations, such as wired networks, where operator-network ownership and location information may be needed by the home network.

In order to preserve user privacy, location information needs to be protected against unauthorized access and distribution. Requirements for access to location information are defined in RFC 3693. That model includes a Location Generator that creates location information, a Location Server that authorizes access to it, a Location Recipient that requests and receives it, and a Rule Maker that provides authorization policies to the Location Server, which enforces access-control policies on requests. Appendix A of the document compares the requirements of a GEOPRIV using protocol with the functionality this document provides.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. RADIUS-specific terminology is borrowed from RFC 2865 and RFC 2866, and terminology related to privacy issues, location information and authorization policy rules is taken from RFC 3693.
sections.plainLanguage: The document fills in the missing half of a location-aware billing system: the network the user is on knows where they are, and this RFC is how that fact reaches the network that charges them, with rules attached.

sections.title: Four Ways to Deliver Location
sections.content:
The document shows four ways location information can be conveyed in RADIUS, assuming that privacy policies allow it.

Out-of-band agreement. The access network attaches location attributes to the Access-Request without an explicit request from the RADIUS server. Such an approach, based on a prior agreement between the RADIUS client and the RADIUS server, is only applicable in certain environments, such as where both are within the same administrative domain. The Basic-Location-Policy-Rules attribute is populated based on the documented defaults unless it has been configured otherwise.

Delivery based on the initial request. If the RADIUS client provides a Location-Capable attribute in the Access-Request, the RADIUS server MAY request location information if it needs that information for authorization and it was not provided. The inclusion of Location-Capable indicates that the NAS is capable of providing location data in response to an Access-Challenge. The Access-Challenge provides a hint about the type of desired location attributes, and the NAS treats the Basic and Extended Location Policy Rules attributes as opaque data, echoing the rules the server provided. The location attributes are then provided in the subsequent Access-Request.

Mid-session request. The on-demand method uses the Change-of-Authorization Request and the CoA-NAK defined in RFC 5176. At any time during the session the Dynamic Authorization Client MAY send a CoA-Request containing session-identification attributes to the NAS. To enable this, the RADIUS server MUST return a Requested-Location-Info attribute with the FUTURE_REQUESTS flag set, together with the Basic and Extended Location Policy Rules attributes in the Access-Accept for the session. On receipt of a CoA-Request with a Service-Type attribute of Authorize Only for the same session, the NAS MUST include location information and echo the previously received policy rules in the subsequent Access-Request. Dynamic authorization is necessary when location is needed on demand and cannot be obtained from accounting information in a timely fashion.

Location in accounting messages. Accounting messages are generated when the session starts, when it stops, and periodically during its lifetime, and may also be generated when the user roams during handoff. Accounting information may be needed by the billing system to calculate the user's bill, for example where different tariffs or tax rates apply based on the location. If the RADIUS server needs location in accounting messages, it needs to include a Requested-Location-Info attribute with the Access-Accept message, and the policy rules attributes are to be echoed in the Accounting-Request if indicated in the Access-Accept.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four timings. The access network can attach location to every sign-in because the two sides agreed to it in advance; the home network can ask for it during sign-in; it can ask for it later in the middle of a session; or it can pick it up with the accounting messages that describe the call.

sections.title: The Operator-Name Attribute
sections.content:
The Operator-Name attribute carries the operator namespace identifier and the operator name. The operator name is combined with the namespace identifier to uniquely identify the owner of an access network. The value is a non-NULL-terminated text whose length MUST NOT exceed 253 bytes, and the attribute SHOULD be sent in Access-Request and Accounting-Request messages where the Acc-Status-Type is set to Start, Interim or Stop. Its RADIUS type is 126 and its length must be at least 4.

The value is a text field of variable length containing an access network operator name, preceded by a one-octet Namespace ID that is encoded in ASCII. The document defines four values for this field, and additional namespace identifiers must be registered with IANA and associated with an organisation responsible for managing the namespace.

TADIG, with identifier 0x30, indicates operator names based on Transferred Account Data Interchange Group codes, which are assigned by the TADIG Working Group within the GSM Association. The TADIG code consists of two fields with a total length of five ASCII characters: a three-character country code and a two-character alphanumeric operator or company ID.

REALM, with identifier 0x31, indicates operator names based on any registered domain name. Such names are required to be unique, and the rights to use a given realm name are obtained coincident with acquiring the rights to use a particular Fully Qualified Domain Name. Since this operator is limited to ASCII, any registered domain name containing non-ASCII characters must be converted to ASCII, and the Punycode encoding is used for this purpose.

E212, with identifier 0x32, indicates operator names based on the Mobile Country Code and Mobile Network Code defined by the ITU. The value consists of three ASCII digits containing the MCC, followed by two or three ASCII digits containing the MNC.

ICC, with identifier 0x33, indicates operator names based on International Telecommunication Union Carrier Codes. ICC values are assigned by national regulatory authorities and coordinated by the ITU. The attribute consists of three uppercase ASCII characters containing a three-letter alphabetic country code, followed by one to six uppercase alphanumeric ASCII characters containing the ICC itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute names the company that owns the access network, so the home network knows who to charge or who to ask for location. Four naming schemes are defined, from mobile carrier codes to domain names, each with a one-character identifier so it can be parsed quickly.

sections.title: Location-Information and Location-Data
sections.content:
The Location-Information attribute MAY be sent in the Access-Request message, the Accounting-Request message, both, or no message. It provides metadata about the location information, such as sighting time, time-to-live and the location-determination method. Its RADIUS type is 127, its length must be at least 23, and the length of the attribute MUST NOT exceed 253 octets.

Its string field holds an Index of 16 bits, a Code of 8 bits, an Entity of 8 bits, a Sighting Time of 64 bits, a Time-to-Live of 64 bits and a Method field of variable length. The Index allows the attribute to provide information relating to the information included in the Location-Data attribute to which it refers. The Code indicates the content of the location profile carried in the Location-Data attribute: two profiles are defined, a civic location profile with the value 0 and a geospatial location profile with the value 1. The Entity encodes which location the attribute refers to: value 0 describes the location of the user's client device and value 1 describes the location of the RADIUS client.

The Sighting Time indicates when the location information was accurate, expressed in the 64-bit Network Time Protocol timestamp format. The Time-to-Live gives a hint for how long the location information should be considered current, also as an NTP timestamp. The Time-to-Live field is different from the Retention Expires field used in the Basic-Location-Policy-Rules attribute, which indicates the time the recipient is no longer permitted to possess the location information. The Method field describes the way the location information was determined and MUST contain the value of exactly one IANA-registered method token.

The Location-Data attribute MAY be sent in Access-Request and Accounting-Request messages. Its RADIUS type is 128 and its length must be at least 5. Its string field holds an Index of 16 bits, which associates the attribute with the Location-Information attributes, followed by the location itself in variable form. The format of the location data depends on the location profile.

The civic location profile corresponds to the value 0 in the Code field. The format is based on the encoding format defined in RFC 4776, except that the first three octets are not put into the Location field, that is the code for the DHCP option, the length of the DHCP option and the what element are not included.

The geospatial location profile corresponds to the value 1. Geospatial location information is encoded as an opaque object, and the format is based on the Location Configuration Information format defined in RFC 3825, but starts with the third octet, so the code for the DHCP option and the length field are not included.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attributes travel together. One says when the location was measured, how long it should be trusted, which of two formats it is in and whether it describes the user or the network equipment. The other carries the location itself, in either a street-address style or a coordinate style, and the index links each one to its partner.

sections.title: The Policy-Rule Attributes
sections.content:
Policy rules control the distribution of location information. The Basic-Location-Policy-Rules attribute MAY be sent in Access-Request, Access-Accept, Access-Challenge, Change-of-Authorization and Accounting-Request messages. RADIUS clients are obligated to use a default value unless explicitly configured otherwise, and to echo the attribute they receive from a server. By default the Note Well field does not carry a pointer to human-readable privacy policies, the retransmission-allowed flag is set to zero, meaning further distribution is not allowed, and the Retention Expires field is set to 24 hours. The attribute reuses work done in RFC 4119 and encodes those policies in a non-XML format. Its RADIUS type is 129 and its length must be at least 12.

Its string field holds a Flags field of 16 bits, a Retention Expires field of 64 bits and a Note Well field of variable length. Only the first bit of the Flags field is defined, the R bit, which corresponds to the Retransmission Allowed field; all reserved bits MUST be zero. When the Retransmission Allowed field is set to zero the recipient of the location object is not permitted to share the enclosed location information, or the object as a whole, with other parties. The value 1 allows the attribute to share the location information with other parties by considering the extended policy rules. The Retention Expires field specifies an absolute time at which the recipient is no longer permitted to possess the location information, expressed as a 64-bit NTP timestamp. The Note Well field contains a URI that points to human-readable privacy instructions; it is useful when location information is distributed to third-party entities, and RADIUS entities are not supposed to process it. Whenever a location object leaves the RADIUS ecosystem the URI in the Note Well attribute MUST be expanded to the human-readable text.

The Extended-Location-Policy-Rules attribute MAY be sent in Access-Request, Access-Accept, Access-Challenge, Access-Reject, Change-of-Authorization and Accounting-Request messages. Its Ruleset Reference field is of variable length and contains a URI indicating where the richer ruleset can be found; the URI SHOULD use the HTTPS scheme. As a deviation from RFC 4119 this field contains only a reference and does not carry an attached extended ruleset, which is motivated by the size limitations imposed by RADIUS. RADIUS clients are obligated to attach the URI when they are explicitly configured to do so, and to echo the attribute they receive from a server; there is no expectation that clients will retrieve data at the URL or parse the XML policies. Its RADIUS type is 130 and its length must be at least 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attributes say what may happen to the location afterwards. The basic one says whether it may be passed on at all, and until when it may be kept; the default is that it may not be passed on and it expires after a day. The extended one points at a longer set of rules kept elsewhere, because the rules will not fit in a RADIUS message.

sections.title: Location-Capable and Requested-Location-Info
sections.content:
The Location-Capable attribute allows an NAS, or the client function of a proxy server, to indicate support for the functionality in this document. The attribute with the value for Location Capable MUST be sent with Access-Request messages if the NAS supports the functionality and is capable of sending location information, and a RADIUS server MUST NOT challenge for location information unless the attribute has been sent to it. Its RADIUS type is 131, its length is 6, and the Integer field encodes the requested capabilities, each capability value representing a bit position. Four capabilities are defined: CIVIC_LOCATION with the numerical value 1, meaning the client can return civic location; GEO_LOCATION with the value 2, meaning it can return geodetic location; USERS_LOCATION with the value 4, meaning it can return the location of the user's client device; and NAS_LOCATION with the value 8, meaning it can return the location of the NAS itself.

The Requested-Location-Info attribute allows the RADIUS server to indicate which location information about which entity it wants to receive. It MAY be sent in an Access-Accept, Access-Challenge or Change-of-Authorization packet, and its RADIUS type is 132 with a length of 6. It uses the same bit positions, plus FUTURE_REQUESTS with the value 16, meaning the client MUST provide future Access-Requests for the same session with the same type of information as returned in the initial Access-Request, and NONE with the value 32, meaning the server asks the client to stop sending location information.

If the server needs location to compute an authorization decision and the client did not provide it, the Requested-Location-Info attribute is attached to the Access-Challenge with a hint about what is required. If the server does not receive the requested information in response to that challenge, it may respond with an Access-Reject carrying an Error-Cause attribute with the Location-Info-Required value. If the server wants location in the Accounting-Request but does not need it for authorization, the Access-Accept MUST include a Required-Info attribute, which is typically the case when location is used only for billing, and the client SHOULD attach location information if available. If the server does not send a Requested-Location-Info attribute, the client MUST NOT attach location information, and the user's authorization policies, if available, MUST be consulted before the server asks for location.

If neither the NAS_LOCATION nor the USERS_LOCATION bit is set, the location of the user's client device is returned by default, if authorization policies allow it. If both are set, the returned location information has to be put into separate attributes. If neither the CIVIC_LOCATION nor the GEO_LOCATION bit is set, no location information is returned, and if both are set the information has to be put into separate attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attributes run the negotiation. The access network says what it can produce, and the home network says what it wants, in bits that say civic or coordinate format and whether the position wanted is that of the user or of the equipment.

sections.title: Using the Same Attributes in Diameter
sections.content:
When used in Diameter, the attributes defined in this specification can be used as Diameter attribute-value pairs from the code space 1-255, the RADIUS attribute-compatibility space, so no additional Diameter code values are allocated. The data types and flag rules for the Diameter AVPs are those defined in RFC 3588: all seven attributes use the OctetString value type, and the flags are the same for each, with MUST NOT set, MAY with the P flag set, MUST NOT unset, and the V and M flags set, and Encr set.

The RADIUS attributes in this specification have no special translation requirements for Diameter-to-RADIUS or RADIUS-to-Diameter gateways; they are copied as is, except for changes relating to headers, alignment and padding. What the specification says about the applicability of the attributes for RADIUS Access-Request packets applies in Diameter to AA-Request or Diameter-EAP-Request. What is said about Access-Challenge applies to AA-Answer or Diameter-EAP-Answer with the Result-Code AVP set to DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH. What is said about Access-Accept applies to AA-Answer or Diameter-EAP-Answer messages that indicate success, and what is said about Access-Reject applies to messages that indicate failure. What is said about CoA-Request applies to Re-Auth-Request, and what is said about Accounting-Request applies to Accounting-Request.
sections.plainLanguage: The same seven attributes work in Diameter, so a network that has moved from RADIUS to Diameter does not need a second set of location rules. The attribute contents are copied unchanged, and each RADIUS message maps onto the Diameter message that does the same job.

sections.title: Protection and Privacy
sections.content:
Requirements for the protection of a location object are defined in RFC 3693: mutual end-point authentication, data object integrity, data object confidentiality and replay protection. If no authentication, integrity and replay protection between the participating RADIUS entities is provided, adversaries can spoof and modify transmitted attributes.

Two mechanisms are proposed for RADIUS. The base RADIUS specification uses a static key, which raised concerns about the lack of dynamic key management. RADIUS over IPsec, defined in RFC 3579, enables standard key-management mechanisms such as KINK, IKE and IKEv2 to establish IPsec security associations. Confidentiality protection MUST be used to prevent an eavesdropper from gaining access to location information, and mutual authentication MUST be provided between neighbouring RADIUS entities to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. The document notes that both requirements are often already met in existing deployments, for instance where EAP is used to carry keying material.

If IPsec protection is not available and RADIUS-specific mechanisms have to be used, the Access-Request message is not integrity protected, which would allow an adversary to change the contents of the location object or to insert, modify and delete attributes or individual fields. To address this the Message-Authenticator can be used to integrity protect the entire Access-Request packet. Access-Request packets including location attributes without a Message-Authenticator SHOULD be silently discarded by the RADIUS server, and Access-Accept messages including location attributes without one SHOULD be silently discarded by the NAS.

On privacy, the document notes that it is possible for the RADIUS server to obtain some location information from the NAS identifier, and that in a number of deployment environments location information about the network also reveals the current location of the user with a certain degree of precision. Three use cases are differentiated: the server does not want location; an out-of-band agreement allows it to be sent without an explicit request; or the server requests it dynamically. The RADIUS client MUST behave as follows: if neither an out-of-band agreement exists nor location information is requested, location information is not disclosed; location information is passed to other entities, such as a local database or log files, only together with the policy rules, and the receiving entity must follow the guidance given with those rules; and the policy rule attributes that are configured must be included in an Access-Request and echoed unmodified in a subsequent Access-Request. The RADIUS server MUST attach the available rules when the client is supposed to provide location information, and MUST attach the privacy rules whenever location information is made available to other entities. A RADIUS proxy, acting as both client and server, MUST follow both sets of rules.

The document also warns that identity and location are tightly coupled. If the identity can be determined by the visited network or RADIUS brokers, location information can be correlated with a particular user, allowing the visited network and brokers to learn movement patterns. Identity can leak through a fixed MAC address or an IP address based on one, through authentication procedures such as CHAP or EAP, through RADIUS returning static data in a Class attribute, through mobility protocols that reveal a long-term identifier such as a home address, and through application-layer protocols that reveal other permanent identifiers. Preventing the correlation of identities with location information requires preventing leakage from all sources, not just one.
sections.plainLanguage: Location is worth protecting as carefully as the credentials. The RFC asks for encrypted transport and mutual authentication between the servers, and it sets strict rules about when the access network may disclose location at all. It also warns that location is only as private as the identity attached to it, so a device with a fixed hardware address undoes much of the protection.

messages.label: Access-Request
messages.note: Carries Location-Capable, saying the access network can produce location.

messages.label: Access-Challenge
messages.note: Carries Requested-Location-Info plus the basic and extended policy rules.

messages.label: Access-Request
messages.note: Now carries Location-Information and Location-Data, and echoes the policy rules.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH ATTRIBUTE MAY APPEAR (RFC 5580, FIGURE 7)

items.label: CIVIC_LOCATION
items.desc: Civic, that is address style, location.

items.label: GEO_LOCATION
items.desc: Geospatial, that is coordinate style, location.

items.label: USERS_LOCATION
items.desc: The location of the user's client device.

items.label: NAS_LOCATION
items.desc: The location of the network access server itself.

items.label: FUTURE_REQUESTS
items.desc: Send the same information in later Access-Requests for the same session.

items.title: No further distribution
items.text: Retransmission Allowed defaults to zero, so the recipient may not pass the location on to other parties.

items.title: Expires after a day
items.text: Retention Expires defaults to 24 hours, the point after which the recipient may no longer keep the information.

items.title: Note Well
items.text: A URI pointing to human-readable privacy instructions, empty by default, which must be expanded to text when the object leaves RADIUS.

items.title: Extended rules by reference
items.text: A URI to a richer ruleset kept outside the message, which the client need not fetch or parse.
